newsitem.title: GUAM: No engine failure in KAL crash, say officials.
newsitem.headline: No engine failure in KAL crash, say officials.

text.p: The Korean Air Lines jumbo jet that ploughed into a hilltop as it tried to land early on Wednesday on this Pacific island did not suffer any engine or structural failure before it crashed, U.S. investigators said on Friday.

The investigators from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) also said the crew were apparently not aware of any problem as the aircraft approached the island's main airport in the dark during a heavy rainstorm.
George Black, leader of the NTSB team investigating the crash, said at a news conference that the cause of the crash was far from being determined.
He discounted media reports that officials had tentatively concluded pilot error was to blame. "Those reports are pure speculation and are based on things that we have not even looked at," he said.

Black also said that 29 of the 254 people on board had survived the crash, contradicting the figure of 27 given earlier by Korean Air Lines and military officials. Black said he could not account for the discrepancy.
In the briefing for reporters, Black painted a picture of a flight proceeding normally, with no sign of impending disaster.
"From what we know at this point, we have no indication that the crew reported anything, any problem," he said.
"There was no indication of engine trouble. There were no missing pieces from the plane."
He also said that the voice recorder tapes, which record conversations in the cockpit, showed that the crew was well aware that the airport's glide path indicator was not functioning.
The system, which aids landing in stormy weather and at night, has been out of service since mid-July and had been the source of speculation as a possible cause of the crash.
Black said that the flight data record showed that the plane was on a controlled, steady descent, and he said there were no signs from the available data that there was any crew fatigue.
